question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:

The chronicles of cartography brim with visionaries whose ambition outstripped mere measurement, transforming the drawing of maps into a meditation on how humankind imagines its place upon the Earth. Each mapmaker — whether charting the monsoon-lashed coasts of the Indian Ocean, the frozen fringes of the Arctic, or the shifting dunes of the Sahara — bequeathed a distinct vision of order wrested from chaos.

Ptolemy, whose Geographia furnished Europe with coordinates for a millennium, fixed the grid of latitude and longitude that later navigators would both revere and revise. Gerardus Mercator, by contrast, contrived a projection that flattered the mariner while distorting the poles, privileging utility over fidelity. The Arab scholar al-Idrisi, commissioned by a Norman king, stitched together the testimonies of far-flung travellers into a tapestry of the known world.

The impulse to map endured into the satellite age, when cartography grew at once ubiquitous and invisible, folded silently into the devices we consult without thought. Thus a map is never a neutral mirror; it is an argument — a quiet assertion about what deserves to be seen, named, and remembered.

 

What is the grammatical role of the clause whose ambition outstripped mere measurement in the opening sentence?
option_3: Noun clause acting as the object
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Adjective (relative) clause modifying "visionaries".

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The clause is introduced by the relative pronoun "whose" and contains its own subject (ambition) and verb (outstripped), so it is a finite relative clause, not a phrase.

 

• A relative clause functions as an adjective: it modifies a noun/pronoun. Here it answers "which visionaries?" and therefore modifies the immediately preceding noun "visionaries".
◦ Example: "The scientist who won the prize spoke." — the underlined relative clause describes "scientist".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Adverbial clause modifying "chronicles": an adverbial clause modifies a verb/adjective and answers when/why/how; "whose" cannot introduce one, and "chronicles" is a noun, not a verb.

 

• Option 3: Noun clause acting as the object: a noun clause would itself be a subject/object; this clause merely describes a noun, so it cannot be one.

 

• Option 4: Adjective phrase modifying "cartography": it is a full clause (subject + verb), not a phrase, and it describes "visionaries", not "cartography".

 

NOTE

 

• Quick test: if the group of words has a subject + finite verb and begins with who/whom/whose/which/that, it is a relative (adjective) clause; without a finite verb it would be a phrase.

Thus a map is never a neutral mirror; it is an argument — a quiet assertion about what deserves to be seen, named, and remembered.

 

In the passage, the word bequeathed most nearly means:
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Handed down to posterity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• To bequeath (विरासत में सौंपना) is to pass something on to those who come after, as one leaves a legacy or inheritance.

 

• In context each mapmaker "bequeathed a distinct vision" — i.e. left behind, for later generations, a way of seeing the world. "Handed down to posterity" captures exactly this transmission of a legacy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Seized forcibly (बलपूर्वक छीनना): opposite idea — bequeathing is giving, not taking.

 

• Option 3: Concealed deliberately (जानबूझकर छिपाना): a bequest is openly left, not hidden.

 

• Option 4: Destroyed utterly (पूर्णतः नष्ट करना): unrelated; a vision is preserved, not annihilated.

 

NOTE

 

• Related words: legacy, inheritance, endowment, testator (one who bequeaths). Do not confuse bequeath (give by will/legacy) with bequest (the thing given).

The impulse to map endured into the satellite age, when cartography grew at once ubiquitous and invisible, folded silently into the devices we consult without thought. Thus a map is never a neutral mirror; it is an argument — a quiet assertion about what deserves to be seen, named, and remembered.

 

What does the word wrested most nearly imply in the phrase "...a distinct vision of order wrested from chaos"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Forcibly obtained through effort.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• To wrest (छीनना / बलपूर्वक प्राप्त करना) means to pull or obtain something by force or with great difficulty.

 

• "Order wrested from chaos" pictures order as won only through struggle against disorder — hence "forcibly obtained through effort".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Gently borrowed: contradicts the force implied by "wrest".

 

• Option 2: Freely donated: the opposite — nothing is given freely here.

 

• Option 4: Accidentally discovered: "wrest" stresses deliberate effort, not accident.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse wrest (to seize by force) with rest (to relax) or wrestle (to grapple, though etymologically linked). Common collocation: "wrest control/power from someone".

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:

The chronicles of cartography brim with visionaries whose ambition outstripped mere measurement, transforming the drawing of maps into a meditation on how humankind imagines its place upon the Earth. Each mapmaker — whether charting the monsoon-lashed coasts of the Indian Ocean, the frozen fringes of the Arctic, or the shifting dunes of the Sahara — bequeathed a distinct vision of order wrested from chaos.

Ptolemy, whose Geographia furnished Europe with coordinates for a millennium, fixed the grid of latitude and longitude that later navigators would both revere and revise. Gerardus Mercator, by contrast, contrived a projection that flattered the mariner while distorting the poles, privileging utility over fidelity. The Arab scholar al-Idrisi, commissioned by a Norman king, stitched together the testimonies of far-flung travellers into a tapestry of the known world.

The impulse to map endured into the satellite age, when cartography grew at once ubiquitous and invisible, folded silently into the devices we consult without thought. Thus a map is never a neutral mirror; it is an argument — a quiet assertion about what deserves to be seen, named, and remembered.

 

Which of the following best summarises the primary argument of the passage?
option_1: Cartography is merely the precise science of measuring distances.
option_2: European mapmakers alone shaped the history of cartography.
option_3: Satellite technology has rendered traditional maps obsolete.
option_4: Maps are not neutral reflections of reality but purposeful arguments shaped by human choices about what to represent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Maps are not neutral reflections of reality but purposeful arguments shaped by human choices about what to represent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage repeatedly frames mapmaking as interpretation, not mere measurement — "a meditation on how humankind imagines its place", Mercator "privileging utility over fidelity", and the closing claim that a map "is an argument".

 

• Option 4 restates this central thesis: maps embody human choices about what "deserves to be seen, named, and remembered".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: the passage explicitly rejects the idea that cartography is "mere measurement".

 

• Option 2: it names the Arab scholar al-Idrisi and non-Western coasts, so it is not Europe-only.

 

• Option 3: satellites make maps "ubiquitous", not obsolete; the point is continuity, not replacement.

 

NOTE

 

• For main-idea questions, prefer the option that covers the whole passage; reject options that are too narrow (a single detail) or contradict the author's stated stance.

Gerardus Mercator, by contrast, contrived a projection that flattered the mariner while distorting the poles, privileging utility over fidelity. The Arab scholar al-Idrisi, commissioned by a Norman king, stitched together the testimonies of far-flung travellers into a tapestry of the known world.

The impulse to map endured into the satellite age, when cartography grew at once ubiquitous and invisible, folded silently into the devices we consult without thought. Thus a map is never a neutral mirror; it is an argument — a quiet assertion about what deserves to be seen, named, and remembered.

 

Which word could best replace ubiquitous in the phrase "...cartography grew at once ubiquitous and invisible..." without significantly changing the meaning?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Omnipresent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ubiquitous (सर्वव्यापी) means present everywhere at the same time. Omnipresent carries the identical sense.

 

• The passage says maps became ubiquitous yet "invisible" (everywhere but unnoticed inside our devices); "omnipresent" preserves that meaning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Transient (क्षणिक): means short-lived — the opposite of being everywhere always.

 

• Option 3: Scarce (दुर्लभ): means rare/in short supply — antonym of ubiquitous.

 

• Option 4: Conspicuous (स्पष्ट/ध्यान खींचने वाला): means highly noticeable — it clashes with the text's "invisible".

 

NOTE

 

• Root: Latin ubique = "everywhere"; omni- = "all". Related: pervasive, universal.

question:
Fill in the blank with the correctly spelt word.

The auditor flagged an ________ violation of the accounting norms.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. egregious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Egregious (घोर/स्पष्ट रूप से बुरा) means outstandingly bad or shocking. The correct spelling is e-g-r-e-g-i-o-u-s ("-gious", not "-geous" or "-gous").

 

• It fits the sentence: an egregious violation = a flagrant, conspicuously bad breach.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: egregeous — wrong: extra "e" ("-geous").

 

• Option 2: egrigious — wrong: "i" for the second "e".

 

• Option 4: egregous — wrong: missing "i".

 

NOTE

 

• Etymology: Latin egregius = "standing out from the flock" (ex- + grex, "flock"). Originally "remarkably good"; now almost always negative.

question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given expression.

A person who remains indifferent to pleasure or pain and endures hardship without complaint.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Stoic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A Stoic (स्थितप्रज्ञ / सुख-दुख में समभाव रखने वाला) is one who accepts pleasure and pain with equanimity and endures difficulty without showing feeling — exactly the definition given.

 

• The word derives from the ancient Greek Stoic school of philosophy, which prized self-control over emotion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Epicurean: one devoted to refined sensual, especially culinary, pleasure — the opposite emphasis.

 

• Option 3: Hedonist: one who believes pleasure is the highest good and pursues it — contrary to indifference.

 

• Option 4: Ascetic: one who practises severe self-denial, usually for religious reasons; abstention, not indifference to pain, is the key idea.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish: Stoic = unmoved by pleasure/pain; Ascetic = self-denying; Hedonist/Epicurean = pleasure-seeking.

question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: TRUCULENT
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Belligerent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Truculent (उग्र/लड़ाकू) means eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant. Belligerent (hostile, combative) is its closest synonym.

 

• Both describe a hostile, quarrelsome temperament.
◦ Example: "His truculent/belligerent reply ended any hope of compromise."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Amiable (मिलनसार): friendly and agreeable — an antonym.

 

• Option 2: Timid (डरपोक): shy, lacking courage — opposite of aggressive.

 

• Option 3: Serene (शांत): calm and untroubled — the reverse of truculent.

 

NOTE

 

• Synonyms of truculent: pugnacious, combative, bellicose, contentious. Root: Latin trux/truc- = "fierce, savage".

question: Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word: TACITURN
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Loquacious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Taciturn (अल्पभाषी/मितभाषी) means reserved and saying very little; habitually silent. Its antonym must convey talkative or fond of speaking.

 

• Loquacious (वाचाल/बातूनी) means tending to talk a great deal; very chatty — the direct opposite of taciturn.
◦ Example: The taciturn clerk barely spoke, while his loquacious partner never stopped chatting.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Reticent (अल्पभाषी/संकोची): unwilling to speak or reveal one's thoughts — a synonym of taciturn.

 

• Option 2: Uncommunicative (कम बोलने वाला): not inclined to talk or share information — a near-synonym.

 

• Option 4: Reserved (संकोची/अल्पभाषी): slow to reveal emotion or opinions — again close to taciturn in sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Trap: three options (reticent, uncommunicative, reserved) are near-synonyms of taciturn; the odd one out is the antonym. Other antonyms: garrulous, voluble, talkative, chatty.

question: Select the correct meaning of the given idiom: Beard the lion in his den
option_1: To flatter a superior in order to gain favours
option_2: To confront a formidable opponent boldly on their own ground
option_3: To avoid a dangerous confrontation at all costs
option_4: To groom or adorn oneself excessively
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To confront a formidable opponent boldly on their own ground.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• To beard the lion in his den means to face a powerful or dangerous person courageously in the very place where they are strongest. Here "beard" is a verb meaning "to confront defiantly".

 

• It stresses boldness in enemy territory.
◦ Example: "She bearded the lion in his den, walking into the CEO's office to demand reform."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: flattering a superior is "to curry favour", a different idiom.

 

• Option 3: the idiom is about facing danger, not avoiding it.

 

• Option 4: it has nothing to do with grooming; "beard" here is figurative.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of confrontation: take the bull by the horns, bell the cat, throw down the gauntlet.

question: Select the correct meaning of the given idiom: Hobson's choice
option_1: A decision made hastily under great pressure
option_2: A choice between two equally undesirable options
option_3: A carefully calculated and profitable gamble
option_4: An apparently free choice that in fact offers no real alternative
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. An apparently free choice that in fact offers no real alternative.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Hobson's choice means a situation in which you seem to be offered a choice, but only one thing is actually available — take it or leave it.

 

• It comes from Thomas Hobson, a Cambridge stable-owner who let customers take the horse nearest the door or none at all.
◦ Example: "With only one supplier in town, we faced a Hobson's choice."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: pressure is not the defining idea; the point is the absence of a real alternative.

 

• Option 2: a choice between two bad options is a dilemma (or "Morton's fork"), not Hobson's choice.

 

• Option 3: it implies no genuine choice at all, let alone a profitable gamble.

 

NOTE

 

• Contrast: Hobson's choice = one option only; dilemma = two undesirable options; Morton's fork = two paths leading to the same bad outcome.

question: Select the correctly spelt word that means 'to clear someone from a charge, blame or accusation'.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Exonerate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Exonerate (दोषमुक्त करना) means to absolve or free from blame. Correct spelling: e-x-o-n-e-r-a-t-e — no "h", with "-ner-" and "-ate".

 

• Usage: "The inquiry exonerated the officer of all charges."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Exhonerate — wrong: no "h" after "ex".

 

• Option 2: Exonorate — wrong: "o" instead of "e" ("-ner-").

 

• Option 4: Exonarate — wrong: "a" instead of "e" ("-ner-").

 

NOTE

 

• Root: Latin ex- ("out of") + onus ("burden") = to remove a burden. Synonyms: absolve, acquit, vindicate, clear.

question: Select the correctly spelt word for the philosophical study of the nature and scope of knowledge.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Epistemology.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Epistemology (ज्ञानमीमांसा) is the branch of philosophy dealing with knowledge — its nature, sources and limits. Correct spelling: e-p-i-s-t-e-m-o-l-o-g-y.

 

• Note the sequence "-steme-" followed by "-ology".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Epistomology — wrong: "o" for the second "e" ("-stom-").

 

• Option 3: Epistimology — wrong: "i" for the second "e" ("-stim-").

 

• Option 4: Epistemulogy — wrong: "-ulogy" instead of "-ology".

 

NOTE

 

• Root: Greek episteme ("knowledge") + logia ("study"). Related terms: ontology (study of being), axiology (study of value).

question: Select the correct one-word substitution for the given expression: 'A person of wide and varied learning across many fields'.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Polymath.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A polymath (बहुश्रुत विद्वान / सर्वज्ञ) is a person whose expertise spans many different subject areas — e.g. Leonardo da Vinci.

 

• The Greek roots — poly ("many") + manthanein ("to learn") — literally mean "having learned much".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Pedant: one who is overly concerned with minor rules or bookish detail — a narrow, not broad, learner.

 

• Option 2: Sycophant: a self-seeking flatterer; nothing to do with learning.

 

• Option 3: Connoisseur: an expert judge in one matter of taste (art, wine), not many fields.

 

NOTE

 

• Related: erudite (adjective, deeply learned), savant, prodigy. A polymath's breadth distinguishes it from a specialist connoisseur.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

She rose to the top of her profession ________ dint of relentless hard work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. by.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "By dint of" is a fixed prepositional phrase meaning "by means of / because of", used to say what enabled an achievement.

 

• The only preposition that combines with "dint of" is by: "by dint of relentless hard work" = through the force of hard work.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: with dint of — not an accepted collocation.

 

• Option 3: in dint of — ungrammatical.

 

• Option 4: through dint of — the sense is right but the idiom fixes on "by", not "through".

 

NOTE

 

• "Dint" once meant "a blow/force". Learn such fixed phrases whole: by virtue of, by means of, by dint of, at the behest of.

question:
Select the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

The committee, along with its chairperson, (1)/ has reviewed every proposal (2)/ but were unable to reach (3)/ a unanimous decision. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3) but were unable to reach.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The grammatical subject is the singular noun "committee". A phrase introduced by "along with" is parenthetical and does not change the number of the subject.

 

• Therefore the verb must stay singular: "...but was unable to reach", to agree with "committee" (as "has reviewed" in part 2 correctly does). "were" is the error.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: correct — the subject and the set-off phrase are properly punctuated.

 

• Option 2: correct — "has reviewed" rightly agrees with the singular "committee".

 

• Option 4: correct — "a unanimous decision" is idiomatic and error-free.

 

NOTE

 

• Rule: phrases like along with, together with, as well as, in addition to, accompanied by are ignored for subject–verb agreement; the verb agrees with the main subject.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in the passive voice.

Who wrote this remarkable novel?
option_1: By whom was this remarkable novel written?
option_2: Who was this remarkable novel written by?
option_3: By whom this remarkable novel was written?
option_4: Who was written this remarkable novel?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. By whom was this remarkable novel written?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• For a "who" question in the active voice, the passive changes the subject "who" to "By whom", and the object becomes the new subject.

 

• Correct passive interrogative order: By whom + was/were + object + past participle? → "By whom was this remarkable novel written?" (past tense → "was ... written").

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "Who ... written by?" is colloquial and, in formal transformation exercises, is not the preferred answer over "By whom".

 

• Option 3: wrong word order — the auxiliary "was" must precede the subject in a question.

 

• Option 4: "Who was written..." reverses the meaning (as if the novel wrote someone) and is ungrammatical.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive of questions: Who → By whom; What/Which → By what/which. Keep the auxiliary before the subject: "By whom was it done?"

question:
Select the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

Each of the participants (1)/ were given a certificate (2)/ and a small token of appreciation (3)/ at the end of the session. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2) were given a certificate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject is "Each of the participants". The pronoun "each" is always singular, regardless of the plural noun in the "of"-phrase that follows it.

 

• Hence the verb must be singular: "...was given a certificate". "were" is the error.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: correct — "Each of the participants" is a well-formed singular subject.

 

• Option 3: correct — the compound object is fine.

 

• Option 4: correct — the adverbial phrase is error-free.

 

NOTE

 

• Always-singular subjects: each, either, neither, every, everyone, everybody, anyone, none (usually), one of. "Each of + plural noun + singular verb."

question:
Select the sentence that uses a homonym of the underlined word — that is, the same word used in a different sense.

The physiotherapist was gentle and tender while treating the injured athlete.
option_1: Her tender words soothed the frightened child.
option_2: He gave her a tender, reassuring smile.
option_3: The mother's tender care nursed him back to health.
option_4: The firm submitted the lowest tender for the construction contract.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The firm submitted the lowest tender for the construction contract.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the given sentence, "tender" is an adjective meaning gentle/caring (कोमल/स्नेहपूर्ण).

 

• A homonym has the same spelling but a different meaning. In Option 4, "tender" is a noun meaning a formal written offer or bid (निविदा) — a completely different sense. That is the required homonym.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all use "tender" in the same "gentle/affectionate" sense as the given sentence, so none is a homonym.

 

• The question asks for a different meaning, which only Option 4 supplies.

 

NOTE

 

• "Tender" has yet another meaning — "to offer formally" (verb: to tender one's resignation) and "legal tender" (money). Other exam homonyms: stern, bark, bank, spring, tender, pupil.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in the active voice.

The new regulations are expected to be implemented by the government next year.
option_1: The government expects implementing the new regulations next year.
option_2: The government will expect to implement the new regulations next year.
option_3: People expect that the government will implement the new regulations next year.
option_4: The government is expected implementing the new regulations next year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. People expect that the government will implement the new regulations next year.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passive "are expected to be implemented" hides the general subject. In the active voice this indefinite agent becomes "people" (or "one"), giving the pattern "People expect that + clause".

 

• The doer inside the clause, "the government", then performs the action: "...the government will implement the new regulations next year", preserving the future sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "expects implementing" is idiomatically wrong; "expect" takes a to-infinitive or a that-clause, not a bare gerund here.

 

• Option 2: "will expect" wrongly shifts the expectation into the future and changes the meaning.

 

• Option 4: still passive ("is expected") and grammatically faulty.

 

NOTE

 

• Standard transformation: "It is expected that S + will..." / "People expect that S + will..." is the active form of "S is/are expected to be..."

question:
Select the most suitable option to replace the underlined part of the sentence.

She solemnly promised to never repeat such a careless mistake.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. never to repeat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "to never repeat" is a split infinitive (the adverb "never" wedged between "to" and "repeat"). In formal SSC usage the adverb is placed before the infinitive: "never to repeat".

 

• "She promised never to repeat such a mistake" is the standard, idiomatic construction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: to repeat never — misplaces the adverb after the verb; unidiomatic.

 

• Option 3: to not ever repeat — clumsy split infinitive with a double negative feel.

 

• Option 4: never repeating — "promise" is followed by a to-infinitive, not a gerund.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs like promise, decide, agree, hope, refuse, resolve take the to-infinitive. Place negatives/adverbs before "to": "decided never to go".

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

He remarked that he would have accepted the offer had they consulted him earlier.
option_1: He said, "If they consult me earlier, I will accept the offer."
option_2: He said, "I will accept the offer if they consulted me earlier."
option_3: He said, "Had they consulted me earlier, I must accept the offer."
option_4: He said, "I would have accepted the offer had they consulted me earlier."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He said, "I would have accepted the offer had they consulted me earlier."

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is a third (unreal past) conditional: "would have accepted ... had they consulted". Such past-perfect conditional forms do not change when moving between direct and indirect speech.

 

• Converting to direct speech, the reporting pronoun "he" reverts to "I" and "him" to "me", giving: I would have accepted the offer had they consulted me earlier.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: wrongly turns it into a first conditional ("consult ... will accept"), changing the meaning.

 

• Option 2: mixes tenses ("will accept ... consulted") — grammatically inconsistent.

 

• Option 3: replaces "would have accepted" with "must accept", distorting the unreal-past meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• Rule: verbs already in the past perfect and would/could/might/should have forms remain unchanged in narration; only pronouns and time/place words shift.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

He said to me, "You must submit the form by tomorrow."
option_1: He told me that I had to submit the form by the next day.
option_2: He told me that I must submit the form by tomorrow.
option_3: He said that you had to submit the form the next day.
option_4: He told me that I have to submit the form by the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He told me that I had to submit the form by the next day.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Three changes are needed: (i) the modal of obligation "must" → "had to" in reported speech; (ii) the pronoun "you" → "I" (it refers to the listener, "me"); (iii) the time word "tomorrow" → "the next day".

 

• "said to me" also becomes "told me" since a listener is mentioned. Result: He told me that I had to submit the form by the next day.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: keeps "must" and "tomorrow" unchanged — backshift not applied.

 

• Option 3: wrongly keeps the pronoun "you" and uses "said" with an object.

 

• Option 4: uses present "have to" instead of the past "had to".

 

NOTE

 

• In narration: must (obligation) → had to; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day; say to → tell. ("must" for general truth/certainty may stay unchanged.)

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph.

1. Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants manufacture their own food using sunlight.

2. The by-product of this reaction, oxygen, is released into the air for other organisms to breathe.

3. In the presence of chlorophyll, they combine carbon dioxide and water into glucose.

4. Thus, this single process underpins nearly all life on the planet.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. 1-3-2-4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 1 is the opening definition ("Photosynthesis is the process...") and must come first.

 

• Sentence 3 explains the mechanism ("they combine carbon dioxide and water") — "they" refers back to the "green plants" of 1.

 

• Sentence 2 then gives the by-product ("The by-product of this reaction, oxygen..."), and Sentence 4 is the concluding generalisation ("Thus...underpins nearly all life"). Order: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (3-1-2-4): starts with "they", whose antecedent has not yet appeared — breaks reference.

 

• Option 2 (1-2-3-4): places the by-product (2) before the mechanism (3), disrupting logic.

 

• Option 4 (3-2-4-1): ends on the definition and opens with an unexplained "they".

 

NOTE

 

• Clues for para-jumbles: a definition/topic sentence opens; pronouns (they/this/it) must follow their noun; a concluding marker (thus, therefore) closes.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences in the correct order to make a logical passage.

1. Consequently, ideas spread across Europe with unprecedented speed.

2. The invention of the printing press revolutionised the dissemination of knowledge.

3. Before it, books were copied laboriously by hand and remained scarce.

4. This democratisation of information helped ignite the Renaissance and the Reformation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-3-1-4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 is the topic sentence introducing the printing press and must open the passage.

 

• Sentence 3 supplies the contrast ("Before it, books were copied... by hand"), where "it" points back to the press in 2.

 

• Sentence 1 states the consequence ("Consequently, ideas spread..."), and Sentence 4 gives the final impact ("This democratisation...ignite the Renaissance"). Order: 2 → 3 → 1 → 4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (3-2-1-4): "Before it" cannot precede the sentence that introduces "it".

 

• Option 3 (2-1-3-4): puts "Consequently" (1) before the contrast (3) that explains the change.

 

• Option 4 (3-1-2-4): again opens with the dependent "Before it", losing the antecedent.

 

NOTE

 

• Link words fix order: Consequently signals an effect (must follow its cause); Before it / This are back-references that need a prior sentence.

question: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 CE by which pair of brothers?
option_2: <style> @font-face { font-family: 'Hari'; src: url('https://static-appxdb-v2.akamai.net.in/fonts/HARI.TTF') format('truetype');} </style>Harihara I and Bukka Raya I
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Harihara I and Bukka Raya I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vijayanagara Empire (विजयनगर साम्राज्य) was founded in 1336 CE by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, who established the Sangama dynasty — the first of the four dynasties that ruled the empire.

 

• Its capital was Hampi (हम्पी) on the banks of the Tungabhadra river, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Karnataka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) of the Tuluva dynasty was the greatest ruler of Vijayanagara; he authored *Amuktamalyada*.

 

• Hasan Gangu (Alauddin Bahman Shah) founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347 — the Deccan rival of Vijayanagara.

 

• Ballala III was a ruler of the Hoysala dynasty, which preceded Vijayanagara in the region.

 

NOTE

 

• The four dynasties of Vijayanagara in order were: Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu. The empire declined after the Battle of Talikota (1565).

question: Which country is popularly known as the 'Land of the Midnight Sun'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Norway.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Norway (नॉर्वे) is called the 'Land of the Midnight Sun' because parts of the country lie north of the Arctic Circle, where the Sun remains visible for 24 hours around the summer solstice.

 

• Its capital is Oslo, and its currency is the Norwegian Krone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Japan is the 'Land of the Rising Sun'; Canada is the 'Land of the Maple Leaf'; Thailand is the 'Land of White Elephants'.

 

• Bhutan is the 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'; Ireland is the 'Emerald Isle'.

 

NOTE

 

• The Midnight Sun phenomenon is also seen in Sweden, Finland, Iceland and northern Russia — all high-latitude regions near the Arctic Circle.

question: Under which scheme does the Government of India provide a minimum monthly pension of ₹3,000 to unorganised sector workers after the age of 60?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maandhan (PM-SYM).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• PM-SYM (प्रधानमंत्री श्रम योगी मानधन) was launched in 2019 by the Ministry of Labour & Employment to give a guaranteed monthly pension of ₹3,000 to unorganised sector workers after they attain 60 years of age.

 

• It is a voluntary and contributory scheme with a 50:50 matching contribution by the beneficiary and the Central Government, for workers with monthly income up to ₹15,000.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Atal Pension Yojana (APY) offers a guaranteed pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 per month based on contribution.

 

• PMJDY is a financial-inclusion scheme for zero-balance bank accounts; PMSBY is an accidental death and disability insurance scheme.

 

NOTE

 

• The nodal agency for PM-SYM is the Life Insurance Corporation (LIC), and enrolment is done through Common Service Centres (CSCs).

question: The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri, built to commemorate a military victory in Gujarat, was constructed by which Mughal emperor?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Akbar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Buland Darwaza (बुलंद दरवाजा), meaning the 'Gate of Magnificence', was built by Akbar around 1575 at Fatehpur Sikri to commemorate his victory over Gujarat.

 

• About 54 metres high, it is one of the tallest gateways in the world and is made of red sandstone with marble inlay.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort and Jama Masjid; he popularised *pietra dura* and the double dome.

 

• Humayun's Tomb in Delhi (built by his widow Bega Begum) is considered a forerunner of the Taj Mahal.

 

NOTE

 

• Fatehpur Sikri was founded by Akbar as his capital; it houses the Tomb of Salim Chishti, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Uttar Pradesh.

question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution, described by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution', guarantees the Right to Constitutional Remedies?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Article 32.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Article 32 (अनुच्छेद 32) confers the Right to Constitutional Remedies, empowering a citizen to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'.

 

• Under it, the Supreme Court can issue five types of writs — Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto (borrowed from English law). It cannot be suspended except during a National Emergency.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Article 14 guarantees equality before law; Article 19 provides the six freedoms (speech, assembly, etc.); Article 21 protects life and personal liberty.

 

• The High Courts can also issue writs under Article 226, which has a wider scope as it covers Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.

 

NOTE

 

• Fundamental Rights are contained in Part III (Articles 12–35) of the Constitution, often called the 'Magna Carta of India', and are borrowed from the Constitution of the USA.

question: Which city hosted the 2024 G20 Leaders' Summit?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The 2024 G20 Leaders' Summit was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 18–19 November 2024, under Brazil's presidency.

 

• The theme of Brazil's presidency was 'Building a Just World and a Sustainable Planet', with a focus on fighting hunger and poverty.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• India hosted the G20 Summit in New Delhi in 2023 at Bharat Mandapam, where the African Union was made a permanent member.

 

• Indonesia hosted the 2022 summit in Bali; South Africa (Johannesburg) held the G20 presidency in 2025.

 

NOTE

 

• The G20 was founded in 1999; the first Leaders' Summit was held in Washington D.C. in 2008. It comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union.

question: The Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant, the largest nuclear power station in India, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Tamil Nadu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant (कुडनकुलम परमाणु ऊर्जा संयंत्र) is situated in the Tirunelveli district of Tamil Nadu and is the largest nuclear power station in India by capacity.

 

• It was built with Russian collaboration (Rosatom) and uses VVER pressurised water reactors.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tarapur (Maharashtra) is India's oldest nuclear power station (commissioned 1969).

 

• Other nuclear stations: Kaiga (Karnataka), Rawatbhata (Rajasthan), Kakrapar (Gujarat), Narora (Uttar Pradesh).

 

NOTE

 

• Nuclear power in India is managed by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), under the Department of Atomic Energy.

question: Which type of soil, rich in iron and lime and formed from Deccan lava, is locally known as 'regur' and is best suited for cotton cultivation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Black soil.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Black soil (काली मिट्टी), also called regur or black cotton soil, is formed from the weathering of Deccan basalt lava and has a high moisture-retention capacity.

 

• It is rich in lime, iron, magnesia and alumina and is ideal for cotton, hence the name 'black cotton soil'. It is found mainly in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and parts of the Deccan Plateau.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Alluvial soil is the most widespread and fertile soil of India, found in the northern plains, ideal for wheat, rice and sugarcane.

 

• Laterite soil forms in high-rainfall regions and is used for growing tea, coffee and cashew.

 

NOTE

 

• Black soil is one of the few soils that develops deep cracks in the dry season, which helps in aeration; it is poor in nitrogen and phosphorus.

question: 'Onam', the grand harvest festival associated with the legendary homecoming of King Mahabali, is the most important festival of which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Kerala.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Onam (ओणम) is the harvest festival of Kerala, celebrated in the Malayalam month of Chingam (August–September), and marks the annual homecoming of the mythical King Mahabali (महाबली).

 

• Key attractions include the flower carpet Pookalam, the grand vegetarian feast Onasadya, and the famous snake-boat race Vallam Kali.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tamil Nadu celebrates the harvest festival Pongal; Karnataka observes Ugadi as its New Year.

 

• Andhra Pradesh and Telangana celebrate Bathukamma and Ugadi as major festivals.

 

NOTE

 

• Onam is celebrated over ten days, from Atham to Thiruvonam, and the traditional dance forms performed include Thiruvathira and the tiger dance Pulikali.

question: Which of the four Vedas is primarily a collection of melodies and chants meant to be sung during rituals, and is regarded as the root of Indian music?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Samaveda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Samaveda (सामवेद) is a collection of melodies and chants (saman) meant to be sung by the Udgatri priest during sacrifices, and is considered the origin of Indian classical music.

 

• Most of its verses are borrowed from the Rigveda but are set to music.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Rigveda is the oldest Veda, a collection of hymns (*rik*); the Yajurveda contains sacrificial formulae (prose and verse).

 

• The Atharvaveda contains spells, charms and remedies of everyday life.

 

NOTE

 

• Each Veda has four parts: Samhita, Brahmana, Aranyaka and Upanishad. The Vedas are called 'Apaurusheya' (not created by humans).

question: In a game of volleyball, what is the maximum number of times a team may touch the ball before it must be returned over the net (excluding a block touch)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Three.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In volleyball (वॉलीबॉल), a team is allowed a maximum of three touches to return the ball across the net, typically as bump–set–spike.

 

• A single player cannot touch the ball twice in succession (except after a block). Each team has six players on the court.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The length of a volleyball court is 18 m and width 9 m; the net height is 2.43 m for men and 2.24 m for women.

 

• Volleyball was invented by William G. Morgan in 1895 in the USA.

 

NOTE

 

• A modern match is played on a rally-point (25-point) system, best of five sets; the defensive specialist wearing a different jersey is called the 'Libero'.

question: The concept of 'Provincial Autonomy' in British India was introduced by which of the following Acts?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Government of India Act, 1935.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Government of India Act, 1935 (भारत शासन अधिनियम 1935) abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced Provincial Autonomy, making provincial ministers responsible to the legislatures.

 

• It also introduced dyarchy at the Centre and provided for an All-India Federation (which never came into being).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms) introduced dyarchy in the provinces and a bicameral central legislature.

 

• The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley–Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates for Muslims.

 

NOTE

 

• The Act of 1935 was the longest Act passed by the British Parliament till then and served as the main source of the Indian Constitution.

question: At which edition of the Olympic Games did Abhinav Bindra win India's first individual Olympic gold medal?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Beijing 2008.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abhinav Bindra (अभिनव बिंद्रा) won India's first individual Olympic gold medal in the 10 m Air Rifle event at the Beijing 2008 Olympics.

 

• It was India's first Olympic gold in an individual event since the country began competing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's first ever Olympic gold came from the men's field hockey team (Amsterdam 1928).

 

• Neeraj Chopra won gold in the javelin throw at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics — India's first athletics gold.

 

NOTE

 

• Abhinav Bindra was awarded the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna and the Padma Bhushan; the Khel Ratna is now called the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award.

question: The Booker Prize-winning novel 'Midnight's Children' was written by which author?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Salman Rushdie.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Midnight's Children' (1981) was written by Salman Rushdie (सलमान रश्दी) and won the Booker Prize in 1981.

 

• It was later awarded the 'Booker of Bookers' as the best novel to have won the prize in its first 25 (and 40) years. The story is set around India's independence at midnight on 15 August 1947.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Arundhati Roy won the Booker Prize in 1997 for *The God of Small Things*.

 

• V. S. Naipaul won the Nobel Prize in Literature (2001); Vikram Seth wrote *A Suitable Boy*.

 

NOTE

 

• Other Booker winners of Indian origin include Kiran Desai (*The Inheritance of Loss*, 2006) and Aravind Adiga (*The White Tiger*, 2008).

question: Which country won the ICC Men's T20 World Cup 2024, defeating South Africa in the final?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• India won the ICC Men's T20 World Cup 2024 by defeating South Africa by 7 runs in the final held at Bridgetown, Barbados, on 29 June 2024.

 

• It was India's second T20 World Cup title (after 2007) and the team finished the tournament unbeaten. The tournament was co-hosted by the West Indies and the USA.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Virat Kohli was named Player of the Match in the final, and Jasprit Bumrah was Player of the Tournament.

 

• Rohit Sharma captained the winning side; Rahul Dravid was the head coach.

 

NOTE

 

• The inaugural ICC T20 World Cup (2007) was also won by India, under the captaincy of MS Dhoni, beating Pakistan in the final.

question: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution is a National Emergency proclaimed?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Article 352.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Article 352 (अनुच्छेद 352) provides for the proclamation of a National Emergency by the President when the security of India is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion.

 

• The term 'armed rebellion' replaced the earlier expression 'internal disturbance' through the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Article 356 deals with President's Rule (State Emergency) due to failure of constitutional machinery in a state.

 

• Article 360 provides for a Financial Emergency.

 

NOTE

 

• A National Emergency has been declared three times in India — in 1962, 1971 and 1975. Emergency provisions (Part XVIII) were borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

question:
Read the following statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct option.

Assertion (A): India's Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) made India the first country in the world to reach the orbit of Mars in its very first attempt.

Reason (R): The Mars Orbiter Mission spacecraft was launched using the PSLV-C25 rocket.
option_1: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true, but R is false
option_4: A is false, but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), also called Mangalyaan (मंगलयान), successfully entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, making India the first country in the world to reach Mars in its maiden attempt and the first Asian nation to reach Martian orbit. So A is true.

 

• MOM was indeed launched on 5 November 2013 aboard the PSLV-C25 rocket, so R is also true — but the choice of launch vehicle does not explain why the mission succeeded on the first attempt. Hence R is not the correct explanation of A.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• MOM was a highly cost-effective mission (about ₹450 crore) and was managed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

 

• The spacecraft carried five scientific payloads, including the Mars Colour Camera and the Methane Sensor for Mars (MSM).

 

NOTE

 

• The PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle) is known as the 'workhorse of ISRO'; MOM used the more powerful XL variant of the PSLV for the interplanetary launch.

question: Which constitutional body, set up under Article 280, recommends the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Union and the States?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Finance Commission.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Finance Commission (वित्त आयोग) is a constitutional body established under Article 280 by the President every fifth year (or earlier).

 

• Its main function is to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Centre and the States (vertical devolution) and among the States (horizontal devolution), and the grants-in-aid to States.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• NITI Aayog is a non-constitutional, non-statutory think tank that replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.

 

• The Inter-State Council is set up under Article 263; the CAG audits government accounts under Article 148.

 

NOTE

 

• The First Finance Commission was set up in 1951 under K. C. Neogy. The 16th Finance Commission is chaired by Arvind Panagariya.

question: Which metal is commonly used for making the filament of an incandescent electric bulb owing to its very high melting point?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Tungsten.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tungsten (टंगस्टन), also called wolfram, is used as the filament of an incandescent bulb because it has the highest melting point of all metals (about 3,410°C) and a high resistivity, so it glows without melting.

 

• The bulb is filled with inert gases like argon and nitrogen to prevent the filament from oxidising and evaporating.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Copper and aluminium are used in electrical wiring due to high conductivity, but their melting points are too low for filaments.

 

• Nichrome (nickel-chromium alloy) is used in heaters and toasters, not bulbs, as it does not glow to give light efficiently.

 

NOTE

 

• Incandescent bulbs are largely being replaced by energy-efficient LEDs and CFLs under India's UJALA scheme.

question: 'Ghoomar' is a traditional folk dance associated with which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Rajasthan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ghoomar (घूमर) is a traditional folk dance of Rajasthan, performed by women in twirling movements while wearing flowing *ghagra* skirts.

 

• It was traditionally performed by the Bhil community and later adopted by the royal Rajput families; it is often performed on festive occasions like Teej and Gangaur.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Garba and Dandiya are folk dances of Gujarat; Bhangra and Giddha belong to Punjab.

 

• Other Rajasthani folk dances include Kalbelia (a UNESCO-listed dance of the Kalbelia tribe) and Kathputli (puppet dance).

 

NOTE

 

• Kalbelia dance of Rajasthan was inscribed in the UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010.

question:
Read the following statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct option.

Assertion (A): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the total market value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory of a country.

Reason (R): GDP includes the net factor income earned by the residents of a country from abroad.
option_1: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true, but R is false
option_4: A is false, but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A is true, but R is false.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• GDP (सकल घरेलू उत्पाद) is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory of a country in a year. So A is true.

 

• GDP does not include net factor income from abroad; it is GNP (Gross National Product) that adds Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) to GDP. So R is false.

 

• The relationship is: GNP = GDP + NFIA.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• NNP = GNP − Depreciation; National Income (NNP at factor cost) = NNP at market price − Net Indirect Taxes.

 

• GDP can be measured by three methods: product (value-added), income and expenditure methods.

 

NOTE

 

• In India, national income estimates are prepared by the National Statistical Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).

question:
Read the following statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct option.

Assertion (A): The ozone layer present in the stratosphere is essential for the survival of life on Earth.

Reason (R): The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation.
option_1: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true, but R is false
option_4: A is false, but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The ozone layer (ओजोन परत) lies in the stratosphere, roughly 15–35 km above the Earth's surface, and shields living organisms from harmful radiation. So A is true.

 

• It does so by absorbing most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays — which is exactly why it is essential for life. So R is true and correctly explains A.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ozone (O₃) depletion is caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), leading to the 'ozone hole' over Antarctica.

 

• The Montreal Protocol (1987) aims to phase out ozone-depleting substances.

 

NOTE

 

• 16 September is observed as the International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer (World Ozone Day).

question: Who is widely regarded as the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. M. S. Swaminathan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• M. S. Swaminathan (ऎम. ऎस. स्वामीनाथन) is known as the 'Father of the Green Revolution in India' for leading the introduction of high-yielding varieties (HYV) of wheat and rice in the 1960s.

 

• The Green Revolution greatly increased India's foodgrain production, making the country self-sufficient. It was most successful in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Norman Borlaug is the 'Father of the Green Revolution' worldwide and won the Nobel Peace Prize (1970).

 

• Verghese Kurien led the White Revolution (Operation Flood) in milk production; William Gaud coined the term 'Green Revolution' in 1968.

 

NOTE

 

• M. S. Swaminathan was awarded the first World Food Prize (1987) and the Padma Vibhushan. He also chaired the National Commission on Farmers.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Jal Jeevan Mission and choose the correct option.

1. It aims to provide Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTC) to every rural household.

2. It was launched in the year 2019.

3. It is implemented by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Only 1 and 2 are correct.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) (जल जीवन मिशन) was launched in 2019 with the goal of providing Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTC) — 'Har Ghar Jal' — to every rural household. Hence statements 1 and 2 are correct.

 

• It is implemented by the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, and not by the Ministry of Agriculture. Hence statement 3 is incorrect.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The mission originally targeted 100% coverage of rural households with tap water supply, with each connection providing at least 55 litres per capita per day (LPCD).

 

• A parallel urban component, JJM (Urban), was launched under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.

 

NOTE

 

• The Ministry of Jal Shakti was created in 2019 by merging the earlier Ministries of Water Resources and Drinking Water & Sanitation.

question: In the context of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), which category enjoys the highest degree of operational and financial autonomy?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Maharatna.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Maharatna (महारत्न) category grants the highest financial and operational autonomy among Central Public Sector Enterprises, allowing a company's board to make large investment decisions (up to ₹5,000 crore or 15% of net worth).

 

• To qualify, a company must first be a Navratna, be listed with a specified public shareholding, and have a high average annual turnover and net profit.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three-tier classification in ascending order of autonomy is Miniratna → Navratna → Maharatna.

 

• Examples of Maharatna companies include ONGC, IOCL, NTPC, SAIL, BHEL, GAIL, Coal India and Power Grid.

 

NOTE

 

• The Navratna scheme was introduced in 1997; the Maharatna status was created in 2010 by the Department of Public Enterprises.
